opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of the most important work, especially in research, feels meaningless at the time you're doing it. When I was a PhD student working on robot learning, there were long stretches where I was building infrastructure, collecting data, debugging simulation environments, things that don't produce a paper or a nice demo. In the moment you ask yourself, why am I spending three months on this? But those foundations end up enabling everything that comes after.

So my attitude is that you have to separate how something feels in the short term from whether it's valuable. Short-term feedback is very noisy. If you only optimize for things that give you an immediate sense of progress, you end up working on incremental problems, because those are the ones that pay off quickly. The bigger questions, like how to get robots to learn general skills from human data, take years before the pieces come together, and much of that time doesn't look like progress from the outside.

That said, I don't think you should blindly do something and hope it pays off. You need some conviction, a reason to believe this matters, even if you can't prove it yet. For me it's a mix of intuition and looking at the trajectory of the field. If I can tell a story about why this piece will matter in five years, I'm comfortable investing in it even when nobody else cares right now.

And honestly, some of those things never pay off, and that's okay too. You learn something, you build skills, and you get better at judging which bets to make. I'd rather take those bets than only do what's guaranteed to look meaningful today.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research work and long-term value generally, but does not say that Danfei Xu was unwilling as a child to do something she found meaningless in the moment.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think a lot of my career has been built on doing things that looked pointless at the time.

When I started working on robot learning, the field was in a strange place. Deep learning was taking off for vision and language, but robots in the real world were still painfully slow, data-hungry, and brittle. People would ask, "Why spend years collecting demonstrations of a robot arm picking up a cup when a hard-coded controller can do it in an afternoon?" And from a short-term, task-completion view, they were right. It was meaningless. We were spending enormous effort to solve problems that had already been solved by other means.

But the point was never the cup. The point was building the infrastructure, the datasets, the simulation tools, the understanding of how imitation and representation learning behave when you put them into a physical system. None of that pays off in a single paper. It pays off five or ten years later when suddenly you have large models that can absorb that kind of data, and the people who did the "meaningless" groundwork are the ones who know what to do with them.

So my honest feeling is a mix of discomfort and conviction. The discomfort is real. When you're in the middle of it, you don't get feedback. Nobody claps for a benchmark that doesn't exist yet or a tool that only three labs use. You have to tolerate looking a little foolish, and you have to keep asking yourself whether you're being patient or just stubborn, because those feel identical from the inside.

What I've learned is to look for a specific kind of signal. If the work is teaching me something I couldn't learn any other way, even when the output seems useless, I keep going. If I'm only continuing because I've already sunk time into it, that's when I worry. The former is an investment. The latter is just inertia dressed up as long-term thinking.

I also tell my students that the long run is made of a lot of short runs that each looked like a waste. Almost every capability we now take for granted in robotics came from someone doing something that their peers thought was a detour. So I try to keep a portion of my time deliberately on things I can't justify yet. Not all of it, because you still have to ship and graduate and get funded. But some of it, protected, specifically because I can't explain why it matters.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses long-term work in robotics and says some groundwork can feel pointless, but does not say Danfei Xu was unwilling as a child to do something she found meaningless despite its anticipated future usefulness.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on why it seems meaningless. Sometimes you’re exploring something and you can’t yet explain where it will lead. That can be valuable—you learn something, gain a different perspective, or discover a question you wouldn’t have thought to ask otherwise.

But I wouldn’t assume that everything will become useful eventually. For me, the question is: am I curious about this, and am I learning from it? If the answer is yes, I’m comfortable giving it some time without knowing the outcome. You need room to explore, but also moments to step back and ask whether it still makes sense to continue.

r001.rationale: The response discusses present-day curiosity and exploration, but does not say that Danfei Xu as a child was unwilling to do something she personally found meaningless at the time, even if it might help in the long run.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be comfortable with not knowing exactly where something will lead. A lot of research feels like that. You try an idea, and maybe it doesn’t work, or you learn something that doesn’t seem useful at the time. But later, when you’re facing a different problem, that experience can become really valuable.

At the same time, I wouldn’t say you should keep doing something just because it might be useful someday. You need to reflect on what you’re learning. If it’s building your understanding or opening up new questions, then even without an immediate result, I think it can be worth doing.
